summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive 3D mission-planning workbench that analyzes solar illumination and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communications for lunar south pole landing sites.

Powered by real NASA LRO LOLA South Pole topography (DEM) and ephemerides verified against JPL Horizons, the web app performs 360° horizon raycasting accounting for lunar curvature. Mission planners can scrub through a 14-day timeline to watch dynamic shadows move across 3D craters, monitor sunset and Earth-occultation countdowns, and compare two sites or launch windows side-by-side (A vs. B) with instant GO/NO-GO viability alerts, Engineer/Explorer modes, and JSON report exports.

At the lunar south pole, the Sun skims the horizon at 1.5°–5°, so minor shifts in coordinates or landing dates can trap a spacecraft in freezing shadows or sever Earth contact. Our tool transforms complex astrodynamics into rapid visual trade-offs, helping teams identify safe, power-sustainable landing zones for Artemis-era missions.
details:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a browser-based tool for planning lunar missions and comparing landing sites. Pick a spot near the Moon’s south pole and a launch date, and it shows how much sunlight you get, how much power that produces, and when you can talk directly to Earth (DTE).

The terrain is a 4 MB elevation file, a 1024x1024 grid at about 72 m per pixel covering a ±37 km radius, built from NASA’s LOLA data. The Sun and Earth positions are computed in the browser with astronomy-engine. We checked them against NASA JPL Horizons, and the Sun’s position agrees to within 0.01 degree.For each site the app casts rays around the full 360° horizon to find what blocks the view, then shows the terrain in 3D with moving shadows and Earth visibility over a 14-day (336-hour) mission. The interface is TypeScript, React, Vite, and Tailwind, Three.js draws the terrain, and Python scripts handle the LOLA processing and the Horizons validation.

The south pole is a rough place to model, and we tried to include everything that makes it rough. There’s no atmosphere, so no refraction bends light over the horizon. The surface curves away. The Sun hovers only 1.5°–2° above the horizon, so a crater rim can shade a whole area, and some of those areas never see sunlight at all (Permanently Shadowed Regions). Earth wobbles along the horizon because of libration, which can cut a communication window short. Each spacecraft also has its own limit for how long it can sit in the dark or lose contact, so the app checks CLPS landers, polar rovers, and Artemis base stations against their own thresholds.

Nothing leaves the user’s device, so there’s no server lag. You can put Scenario A next to Scenario B and watch the differences update live, with countdowns to sunset and Earthset and a GO / CAUTION / NO-GO verdict.

We also built it for two audiences. Engineer mode takes custom coordinates and hardware profiles, and exports JSON telemetry. Explorer mode is a game of “rescue the mission” challenges. Delay a launch by 14 days, or nudge the landing coordinates a little, and a sunlit peak becomes a frozen shadow trap. It’s a quick way to see why lunar site selection is so hard.

A GIS analysis that would eat an afternoon takes a few seconds here, so mission planners can rerun the numbers when a schedule or target changes. Students and teachers get a feel for the problem without needing the GIS background.
